subject: Indexing a lookup table in Stan

messages.author: abab84dd2ba42997
messages.subject: Indexing a lookup table in Stan
parts:
Hi Stan users,

Short question: does Stan have a function to return the index corresponding to the minimum value of a vector (i.e. argmin / which.min)? It doesn't appear to from the manual. If not, can anyone suggest a workaround for this? There is a thread with similar overtones here but it doesn't appear to offer the solution I'm looking for.

Background: My model contains a link function that is costly to compute. The link function takes an input value x and deterministically returns a new value y. The new value y doesn't depend on model parameters or data, only on x (which *does* depend on model parameters). Therefore, I thought would make sense to generate a lookup table of x and y values offline, pass this lookup table to Stan in the data block, and have Stan lookup y from its computed x value.

To do this in Python or R, I would subtract the (scalar) value of x from my lookup vector of x values (lookup_x), then use argmin / which.min to return the index of the lookup vector corresponding to the smallest absolute difference between x and lookup_x. I can then return y by indexing the lookup_y value corresponding to that index.

pseudocode:

diff = lookup_x - x
idx = argmin(abs(diff))
return lookup_y[idx]

Can anyone suggest how to do this in Stan?

Follow-up question: will using a lookup table in this fashion interfere with Stan's use of gradients? I could imagine that depending on the precision of my lookup table, I will need to turn down the tolerance on any gradient descent Stan is running. Suggestions or thoughts?

Thanks in advance,

Tom

messages.author: abab84dd2ba42997
messages.subject: Re: Indexing a lookup table in Stan
parts:
Ok, here's a first attempt using a loop (adapted from here). This defines a function in the function block:

    real lookup_fun(real x, int L, vector lookup_x, vector lookup_y){
        # return a y value from the lookup table corresponding to a given
        # x, lookup table vectors and the length of the lookup
        # table L.
        # assumes there is only one min.
        int min_idx;
        vector[L] diff;

        diff <- lookup_x - x;
        min_idx <- 1;

        for (i in 1:L){
            # absolute val only works for reals, not vector.
            diff[i] <- fabs(diff[i]);
            if (diff[i] < diff[min_idx]) {
                min_idx <- i;
            }

        # return corresponding y:
        return lookup_y[min_idx];
        }
    }

My model compiles and returns reasonable-looking values, but any advice on what problems I could be generating in the gradients by using a lookup table would be greatly appreciated.

Tom

messages.subject: Re: Indexing a lookup table in Stan
parts: My model compiles and returns reasonable-looking values

False. The values returned by the model never seem to move beyond the prior -- that is, somehow the parameters are not being updated.

This seems to be that I'm using my (user-defined) functions incorrectly. In model_1.stan (attached), the model compiles and samples fine, but the parameter values never move away from the priors - like they're not being updated by the data. I guess this is a problem with me not understanding function scoping in Stan, because when I pull the code out of the functions and put it in the model block (see model_2.stan), this model seems to run. 

However, model_2.stan samples *extremely* slowly (as in, each iteration takes an extremely long time). I suspect this is because the gradients are too coarse, due to my lookup table. Does anyone have a suggestion as to how to improve this?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Indexing a lookup table in Stan
parts:
It’s not that the gradients are too coarse it’s that they don’t exist
(essentially the point where you map input -> index is discontinuous
and the discontinuity propagates through the rest of the gradient).

If this is a low-dimensional link function then I would consider
using a Gaussian process as a smooth, fast emulator, although
these can easily stray from the the true function after a few
dimensions so you have to be very vigilant.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Indexing a lookup table in Stan
parts:
If there’s a good function approximation that’s your best bet.

For posterity the GP would look something like

// put weakly informative priors on GP hyperparameters
// construct covariance matrix, Sigma, from training covariates
// add a gaussian process prior on the training data, y ~ normal(0, Sigma)
// use hyperparameters to construct predictive distribution for new y given new x
// use predictive y to model expensive function

You fit the GP to the training data and incorporate it into your
model at the same time, which maximizes the information.
